title: The staleness sweep: how much staleness a run tolerates, with and without the correction
design_ref: When off-policy helps or hurts; building intuition: off-policy experiments
purpose: Run the design's standard experiment: staleness from 0 to 15 versions, naive and decoupled correction, two learning rates, two seeds, as one Indexed Job on the research queue at low priority. Turn the 40 runs into the staleness curve and a reference table that answers 'can I set staleness to 8?'.

steps.display: # sweep staleness-sweep-s03: 40 cells read back from the state bucket (already complete)
python sweep_table.py staleness-sweep-s03   # one row per cell of the grid, averaged over the two seeds; K is the number of versions one batch of samples feeds
python reference_lookup.py --lr 1e-5 --staleness 8   # the lookup the library answers
steps.output:
K= 1 (max age  0): decoupled 0.302   naive 0.334   behavior KL 0.0006
K= 2 (max age  1): decoupled 0.475   naive 0.391   behavior KL 0.0028
K= 4 (max age  3): decoupled 0.435   naive 0.421   behavior KL 0.0057
K= 8 (max age  7): decoupled 0.478   naive 0.440   behavior KL 0.0106
K=16 (max age 15): decoupled 0.408   naive 0.434   behavior KL 0.0194

checks.description: all forty cells completed through the research queue
checks.because: One Indexed Job, one pod per cell, admitted by Kueue at sweep-low priority. A cell that dies would leave a gap in the grid, so completeness is checked, not assumed.

checks.description: no cell trained on a sample older than its limit (maximum age equals K - 1)
checks.because: The age of every trained micro-batch is recorded. The run regenerates as soon as the next sample would be older than the limit.

checks.description: the behavior KL rises with every step up in K, at both learning rates
checks.because: More versions per batch means older samples on average, and the KL between behavior and target grows with age (S02). K=16 is 3.6 times K=2 at lr 3e-6, 7.0 times K=2 at lr 1e-5.

checks.description: the measurement is repeatable at the stable learning rate: the two seeds of a cell end within 0.10 of each other, in every cell
checks.because: The largest spread among the ten cells at 3e-6 is 0.071. Differences between settings smaller than that are not read as findings anywhere in this appendix.

checks.description: the reference library covers the whole grid and is stored with the recipe
checks.because: A table of (learning rate, correction, staleness) to held-out score, with the model, the task, the step count and how many runs collapsed, is what 'can I set staleness to 8?' is answered from.

notes: Averaged over the grid, naive minus decoupled held-out pass rate is -0.008, against a seed spread of up to 0.141: at zero engine mismatch the two losses are not told apart here (S05 adds the mismatch).

Predictions written down before the sweep, from a one-seed pilot, and what the sweep said. (1) At the smaller learning rate, K=16 within 0.05 of K=1: FAILED (K=1 0.561, K=16 0.502, a cost of 0.060 that grows with K; K up to 4 is within 0.016 of K=1). (2) At the larger rate, K=16 at least 0.03 below K=1: FAILED (K=1 0.302, K=16 0.408: the run with no staleness is the one that collapsed in both seeds. A likely cause, which I did not isolate with an ablation: a stale token is outside the trust region more often (2.8% of tokens clipped at K=16, none at K=1) and a clipped token carries no gradient, so the clip that makes stale data safe also brakes the step). (3) A larger K at least 20% cheaper per step: FAILED (L40S, 3.98 s at K=1, 4.23 s at K=16: generation is a small share of a step on this model and these short answers, so there is little for staleness to hide).
